title: Bram and the Well
premise: Folklorist Petra Ravensworth returns to the village of Hollowmere to record its founding songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice—and to discover that Bram, the imaginary friend who vanished when he was nine, is waiting on his porch, unchanged after twenty years. Bram reveals the founders bound something beneath the old well with a song, and the binding weakens every time a verse goes unsung; Petra's own family were the keepers who let it lapse. As the well-thing wears the faces and voices of villagers to lure him closer, Petra must choose between loyalty to Bram—who may be the binding's first victim or its first offering—and the truth that finishing the ritual requires a keeper willing to be sung into the dark. In the end Petra completes the song at the well's mouth, learns Bram was the previous keeper's child taken as payment, and steps down willingly in Bram's place, leaving Hollowmere silent, whole, and finally able to sing every verse twice.
about_author: Bram Nystrom grew up in a coastal village where certain hymns were sung only once a year, and never after dark. A former archivist of oral histories, he writes horror about the debts communities pass down like heirlooms.

chapters.title: The Verse They Won't Repeat
chapters.summary: Petra Ravensworth arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and seven years of rationalizations. Villagers give him one verse each, then go quiet—old Marta weeps mid-line and slams her door. On his porch that night sits Bram, exactly as he left him at age nine, asking why it took so long. POV: Petra. Emotional beat: uncanny homecoming, the collapse of his careful skepticism.

chapters.title: What the Founders Owed
chapters.summary: In the church archive, Petra finds his grandmother's handwriting in the founders' ledger: the well-song binds 'the patient guest,' renewed by a keeper singing all verses aloud. Bram admits he remembers being sung down the well once—but not by whom. That night Petra records a villager humming the forbidden final verse, and the tape plays back with an extra voice answering. POV: Petra. Emotional beat: dread deepening into complicity.

chapters.title: The Well Sings Back
chapters.summary: The thing beneath begins wearing familiar voices—Marta's dead son calling from hedges, Petra's mother from the well itself. Bram grows translucent whenever a verse is sung wrong, forcing Petra to confront that Bram may be sustained by the failing ritual rather than freed by it. When Petra refuses to sing, the village's livestock stills and children sleepwalk toward the water. POV: Petra, with one interlude in Bram's fragmentary memory. Emotional beat: loyalty fracturing against truth.

chapters.title: Every Verse, Twice
chapters.summary: At the well on solstice night, Petra sings the complete song while the thing offers him everyone he has ever missed. He understands at last: Bram was the last keeper's child, payment made a generation ago, and the ritual demands a willing keeper now. Petra finishes the final verse twice, takes Bram's hand, and descends together—the debt paid in company rather than alone. Epilogue: Marta sings the whole song through, twice, smiling. POV: Petra. Emotional beat: sacrifice transmuted into belonging.
